children.text: Packing for a dahabiya differs from a normal hotel stay.

The cabin is comfortable; storage is limited. The day doesn't close inside the same hotel — you land at temples, walk the riverbank, take the wind on deck, and adjust to morning-evening temperature gaps. What's needed isn't many clothes but a small set that works well.
A dahabiya is a boat that changes the pace at which you see the Nile. Matching luggage to that pace makes the trip easier.
A soft bag
Avoid a hard, large suitcase first.

A dahabiya cabin doesn't have a wide hotel-style luggage area. You board via wood gangways or from the riverbank at times. A large wheeled suitcase, convenient at the airport, takes space and is hard to move on the boat.
A medium soft bag per person — ideally a duffel or soft-type travel bag — handles best. Fits under the bed or in a corner, without spreading luggage.
On a dahabiya, you handle everything brought inside your own space. Starting with less is part of comfort.
Layers for clothing
Between
Luxor
and
Aswan
, day and night feel differ.

In the main October-to-March travel season, midday temple visits are warm; evening on deck can suddenly cool. December to February especially, don't underestimate post-sunset river breeze. "Egypt trip means thin clothing" isn't always right.
The base is thin long-sleeve shirts, light trousers, and a layer to throw on. Linen, light cotton, and quick-dry blends work well; pale colours suit sun and dust.
For evenings, a thin fleece, light jacket, or packable warm layer is reassuring. Some boats provide blankets; don't premise on it.
After April, in heat, covering skin with thin long fabric is more practical than showing. At temples, covering shoulders and knees is natural; under strong sun, the body is easier too.
Three pairs of shoes is enough
On a dahabiya trip, the shoe difference shows on shore more than on board.
Temple floors look flat but include stone, sand, steps, and worn stairs. At Karnak,
Edfu
Kom Ombo
, Philae, and Luxor west-bank sites, you use the feet more than appearances suggest.
If packing, first one pair of walking shoes. Light walking shoes with covered toes or anti-slip trail shoes are useful.
Next, one pair of solid sandals. Not beach flips — sandals that fix the foot. Use on board, short shore stops, and on hot days.
Finally, light footwear for going between cabin and deck is easy. You don't need to wear solid shoes each time on board.
Don't cut sun protection
Upper Egyptian sun is strong, and the Nile's surface reflects light. Deck breeze can feel cool while sunburn quietly progresses.
Carry high-SPF sunscreen and use before morning sightseeing and before long deck time. Beyond face, neck, ears, and back of hands are easy to forget.
A wide-brim hat fits. A baseball cap alone doesn't protect ears or neck. Sunglasses are practical too. Reflection off water and stone ties directly to long-day fatigue.
A thin scarf is one of the hardest-working small items on a dahabiya trip. Sun cover, cold cover, covering at religious sites or in town, sand and wind cover. Pack a light one, ideally two.
A small medical kit
A dahabiya doesn't go into uninhabited zones.
Esna
, Edfu, Kom Ombo, and Aswan have towns. You can't always buy what you need easily on the spot.

Carry prescription medicine a little beyond the day count. Painkillers, stomach medicine, bandages, antiseptic, oral rehydration salts, and antihistamines reassure. On a hot temple-visit day, fluid loss comes faster than expected.
Add insect repellent. On the Nile, mosquitoes can rise in the evening into night. Practical especially for those eating or reading on deck.
Hand sanitiser and wet wipes help too. At sites, landings, and short village walks, hand-washing isn't always immediately near.
Documents and cash
Passport, visa documents, travel insurance, and emergency contacts — beyond inside the phone, hold paper copies too. On river transfers, don't rely entirely on signal and battery.
Cash is needed. In Luxor and Aswan, cards and ATMs work in more places; between them, for small payments, tips, drinks, village shopping, and short transfers, Egyptian pound cash is practical.
Mix small notes with large notes for easier payment. Arranging in Luxor or Aswan before boarding is realistic.
Camera and power
A dahabiya trip is heavy on photo time.

Morning river, evening cliffs, fields from the deck, small places where the boat stops. Beyond big sites, the transfer itself becomes subject. Modern smartphones suffice often; for birds and far-bank scenery, a light camera with telephoto adds enjoyment.
Always carry a power bank. Even with cabin charging, a long sightseeing day drains the phone first. Don't forget charging cables, plug adapters, and spare memory cards if needed.
A small waterproof pouch for phone or camera helps with water-edge boarding and disembarking.
What not to bring
Formal clothes aren't really needed on a dahabiya.
Dinner can have a proper atmosphere; what's asked isn't suit or dress but clean and settled attire. Linen shirt, light dress, thin long trousers suffice.
Heavy guidebooks become luggage. Carry needed parts in electronic form or one thin reading book. On deck, books matching the trip's pace stay more than information-heavy ones.
You don't need many pairs of jeans. Heavy, slow-drying, uncomfortable on hot days. One at most.
Exercise gear is usually unused. A dahabiya trip looks like sitting; at sites you walk well. To move the body, walking the deck morning or evening is more natural.
For temple visits
Dahabiya routes visit temples like Edfu, Kom Ombo, Esna, and Philae. Some boats stop at places like El Kab or
Gebel el-Silsila
Dress isn't hard. Cover shoulders and knees. Walk easily in heat. Stable shoes. Those three suffice.
In a small day bag, put water, sunscreen, hat, scarf, phone, paper tickets or documents, and small cash. Not "back at the cabin if needed" — have what you need while on shore.
Why pack light
A dahabiya is a boat that strips extras from the trip slowly.
No large-hotel storage. No large-ship facilities. There's cabin, deck, river, port stops, and time.
The less luggage, the better this trip works. Morning landings ease, the cabin doesn't scatter, and attention turns to deck time.
Bring what's needed. Leave what isn't.
Packing for a dahabiya is just that. River trips read better when light.

deck: On a dahabiya trip, judgment matters more than volume. Cabins, temples, sun, evening cool, river transfer — what you actually need.
